paragraphs.heading: Ocean or sea
paragraphs.text: Used on their own, "the ocean" and "the sea" both mean the interconnected body of salt water that covers the majority of Earth's surface. Strictly speaking, a sea is a body of water partly or fully enclosed by land, and generally a division of the world ocean. There is no sharp line between seas and oceans, though seas are generally smaller. The present-day term World Ocean dates from the early 20th century, when the Russian oceanographer Yuly Shokalsky coined it.

paragraphs.heading: Zones by depth and light
paragraphs.text: Ocean scientists divide the ocean into zones, both vertical and horizontal, according to physical and biological conditions. The pelagic zone is the water column of the open ocean, from the surface to the ocean floor. That column is divided further by depth and by how much daytime sunlight is present. The photic zone starts at the surface and reaches the depth where light is only 1% as strong as at the surface, roughly 200 m in the open ocean. This is the zone where photosynthesis can occur.

paragraphs.heading: Life near the surface
paragraphs.text: In photosynthesis, plants and microscopic algae take light, water, carbon dioxide and nutrients and make organic matter. As a result, the photic zone is the zone with the most biodiversity and the source of the food that sustains most of the ocean ecosystem. Light can reach only a few hundred metres further down. Below that, the deeper ocean is cold and dark. Over 230,000 species are known to live in the ocean, and it may hold perhaps over two million.

paragraphs.heading: Warm top, cold depths
paragraphs.text: Ocean temperatures depend on how much solar radiation reaches the surface. In the tropics, surface temperatures can rise above 30 °C. Close to the poles, where sea ice forms, the equilibrium temperature is about −2 °C. Deep water in every part of the ocean is between −2 °C and 5 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Currents
paragraphs.text: Water in the ocean circulates constantly, and that creates ocean currents. The forces behind them include differences in temperature and salinity, wind and the Coriolis effect. Tidal currents come from tides, and surface currents from wind and waves. The Gulf Stream and the Antarctic Circumpolar Current are two of the major ones. Currents carry massive amounts of water, heat, gases and pollutants around the world, and also from the surface down into the deep ocean, and all this affects the global climate system.

paragraphs.heading: Dissolved gases
paragraphs.text: Ocean water holds dissolved gases, including oxygen, carbon dioxide and nitrogen, and these are exchanged at the surface. How well they dissolve depends on the temperature and salinity of the water. The amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is rising because of CO₂ emissions, mainly from burning fossil fuels. The oceans absorb CO₂ from the atmosphere, so a higher concentration leads to ocean acidification, which is a drop in pH value.

paragraphs.heading: People and the ocean
paragraphs.text: The ocean gives people seafood, other marine resources and a way to transport things. Human activity is mostly coastal, and the continental shelf and coastal waters are the parts most affected by it. The ocean faces many environmental threats, among them marine pollution, overfishing and the effects of climate change. Those effects include a warming ocean, ocean acidification and rising sea level.
